docTitle: Addictive design and the EU: LinkedIn carousel

slides.title:
The EU says
addictive feed
design may
break *the law.*
slides.sub: Preliminary findings against TikTok (6 Feb 2026) and Instagram and Facebook (10 Jul 2026). Plus 5 questions for your next design review.

slides.title:
Not the content.
The *design.*
slides.takeaway: Under the Digital Services Act, the Commission named infinite scroll, autoplay, push notifications and highly personalised recommendations.

slides.title:
Change the
*defaults.*

rows.head: Infinite scroll: off
rows.sub: Meta: off by default. TikTok: phase it out.

slides.takeaway: Both findings are preliminary. TikTok called its finding “categorically false and entirely meritless”.
slides.source: EC press releases, Feb and Jul 2026; TikTok via AP

slides.title:
Old formats had
*stopping points.*
slides.takeaway: Chapters, episodes, a Next page button. Infinite scroll (Aza Raskin, 2006) and autoplay took those stopping points away.

slides.title:
Notifications:
one week on,
one week _off._
slides.takeaway: Notifications are a design choice too. In a CHI 2016 study, 221 people spent one week each way; the “on” week brought more self-reported symptoms.
slides.source: Kushlev, Proulx and Dunn, “Silence Your Phones”, CHI 2016

slides.title:
Behaviour =
motivation, ability,
*prompt.*
slides.lede: B.J. Fogg's Behavior Model (Stanford). The features on the earlier pages each supply one of the three.

rows.head: Ability: one tap opens the app
Is this default good for the user, or for time in the app?
Does this notification help, or just bring people back?
Can people turn it off in one step?
Could we defend it to a regulator?

slides.title:
Which one would
your product fail?
slides.body: I made a video on the design choices that keep people scrolling, and where they came from. Tell me in the comments.
